title: Choosing friends
hookLine: good company shapes a young life
tomorrow: Fateh picks his very first seva. what does he choose?

cards: Fateh has a new best friend, Leo, and Leo is fun. Leo is also the reason Fateh has started leaving the quiet kid out at lunch, because Leo says he's weird. Fateh tells Simran this on a walk, proud of how cool Leo is.
Simran wants to say: drop him. Maya, walking with them, says her grandma had a line for this. Two traditions, it turns out, have a picture for exactly this.

teach.h: DO FRIENDS SHAPE WHO YOU BECOME?
teach.b: The question is old: do the people around you shape who you become? Kabir answers with a tree, in a salok on ang 1365.

In paraphrase: the sandalwood tree is good, though ordinary trees grow around it; they stayed close to the sandalwood, and became fragrant like it. Good company works by nearness. You pick up its scent without trying.

Maya's grandma's line comes from the book of Proverbs, read by Jews and Christians alike. In the King James Bible: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed."
That's real shared ground. Both say company changes you, whether you notice or not. And one honest difference.
Proverbs is advice about choosing: walk with the wise, and steer clear of fools.
Kabir's sandalwood doesn't choose its neighbors at all. The ordinary trees are already growing there, and it changes them.

Sikhs hear both in the idea of sangat: seek out good company, and be good company for whoever is near. So Simran doesn't say drop him. She asks Fateh one question: when you're with Leo, who do you turn into?
And whose lunch table could use some sandalwood?

how: Sikh parents speak of sangat, good company, and encourage young people to spend time with friends who bring out the best in them, at the gurdwara, at camps and at school.

o: letting your parents pick who you spend time with
keeping only friends from your own community
seeking friends who make you better, and being one

games.q: two pictures of friendship — tap the pairs.
p: makes the trees beside it fragrant
walk with wise men and be wise

s: the Granth's only advice about friends is to cut off bad ones
Kabir's sandalwood changes the trees already around it; good company spreads by nearness.
Proverbs and Kabir both say company changes you
shared ground, in each tradition's own words.
Kabir's sandalwood salok tells you to pick your neighbors carefully
the ordinary trees are already there. the point is that nearness to the good changes them.

games.q: your teenager's closest friend is fun but keeps pulling her away from her old friends. going by today, what's the move?
o: ban the friend; one bad influence ruins everything.
stay out of it; friends don't really change who you are.
ask her who she turns into around this friend, and keep good company close.
games.why: both Kabir and Proverbs say company shapes you. Simran didn't say drop him; she asked Fateh who he becomes around Leo.

practice: Think of one friend whose company makes you a little better: kinder, braver, more honest. Send them a short message saying so, plainly. Then sit, and notice what it was about being near them that rubbed off.

wordCard.voice: Choosing friends. Seeking company that makes you better, and being that company for whoever is near.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chandan, sandalwood; in Kabir's salok, it makes the trees beside it fragrant.

carryVoice: Your line: good company. For the dinner table: who do you turn into around your friends? Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 1365 (Salok Kabir: kabeer chandan kaa birvaa bhalaa berrhio dhaak palaas; oe bhee chandan hoe rahe base jo chandan paas), paraphrased
